doc.title: Charles Calello interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 21, 2025

title: Being a cog in the wheel and stealing like professionals
summary: He describes arrangers as part of a team, standing on others' shoulders, drawing on Krall, Basie and Nelson Riddle.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Right. Well this has just been a delight for me, as an arranger myself I’m very envious of your career. And another quote – one more quote from you. “I was one of the cogs in the wheel of record producing.” You were a large cog I think.

Well you know the position that arrangers have, it’s sort of like the drummer who gets the groove on a record, and a bass player who reads the notes but makes it feel like it’s in the pocket. Any one of those guys missing could alter the outcome. And when you’re working with a team and you’re a cog in the wheel, you’re one of the ones that’s making that wheel turn. Now in some cases yeah you play a more major part than this person over here or that person over there. But in essence pretty much everything we do as arrangers, we’re standing on somebody’s shoulders. So as far as our being original, we never really take total credit for being original because as John Lennon once said, “The difference between professionals and amateurs, amateurs copy and professionals steal.” The thing about writing, in my mind I want the rhythm section to sound like a Diana Krall record, I want the horns to sound like a Basie record, and I want the strings to sound like Nelson wrote them. Now how do I put that together? So you’re constantly picking pieces and regurgitating them back to the paper. So, in your brain you’re a cog. I don't know if that makes any sense.
